title: ‘Operation Safed Sagar’: Inside Netflix’s High-Altitude Bet on the Untold Story of the India-Pakistan Kargil War
description:
The most important prop in Netflix series “Operation Safed Sagar” isn’t a fighter jet. It’s a wing badge.

	When creator and showrunner Abhijeet Sin
body:
The most important prop in Netflix series “Operation Safed Sagar” isn’t a fighter jet. It’s a wing badge.

	When creator and showrunner Abhijeet Singh Parmar first sat down with Alka Ahuja – widow of Squadron Leader Ajay Ahuja, who was killed in the 1999 Kargil War – he and his team arrived with a list of some 70 to 100 questions. They asked none of them. Every wall of her home was, in his words, a museum to her husband: a medal here, a trophy there, a photograph on every surface. All the team could offer was an open invitation for her to speak.
	

	“All we asked her was, ‘Ma’am, whatever you want to tell us about sir,'” Parmar says. What she told them became part of “Operation Safed Sagar,” and Ahuja later entrusted the production with her husband’s original wing badge, now worn on screen by star Siddharth. “I know that rather than having just a very good story to tell, this is also a huge responsibility in someone’s real life,” Parmar adds.


	That gesture of trust threads through Netflix India‘s six-episode series, which premiered on Thursday at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi ahead of its Friday streaming release. Created and showrun by Parmar and Kushal Srivastava, directed by Oni Sen and produced by Matchbox Shots LLP and Feel Good Films, the show follows a brotherhood of fighter pilots and the political maneuvering behind enemy lines as India mounts what became the world’s highest air operation. It dramatizes the Indian Air Force’s role in the Kargil War, the 1999 conflict fought in the high-altitude Kargil district of Jammu and Kashmir after Pakistani soldiers and militants crossed the Line of Control and occupied positions on the Indian side, a chapter Netflix says has rarely been explored on screen given that most prior portrayals centered on the Army.
	

	Speaking at the premiere, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos framed the series as an emblem of the streamer’s decade in the country, tying its scale to a broader economic case for local production. He said the show contributed more than $24 million to the Indian economy, with VFX and creative-tech work alone accounting for more than $5 million, or roughly 20% of the total. 

	“Behind every episode are thousands of people whose creativity, skill and dedication make that story possible,” Sarandos said. “The scale of this series and the production demonstrates that India today has the talent, the technical expertise and the production capabilities to create entertainment that stands confidently alongside the very best in the world.” He added that the milestone extends “The Netflix Effect” the company has tracked across its Indian slate for 10 years.

	The series’ key cast includes Siddharth, Jimmy Shergill, Abhay Verma, Dia Mirza, Prajakta Koli, Adil Hussain, Mihir Ahuja, Taaruk Raina, Arnav Bhasin and Amrita Bagchi, with a score featuring composers Amit Trivedi, Vishal Dadlani, Supinwal Singh and Anurag Saikya. 



	

					“Operation Safed Sagar”
									Netflix
	



	“There are times when you choose a story, and there are times when the story chooses you,” Parmar says of how “Operation Safed Sagar” came together. The project began, he says, over cups of tea. Srivastava, his co-creator, served in the Air Force for six years after the Kargil War and brought Parmar story after story the writer had never encountered in his own research: “Bounce,” a house entry ritual in which junior officers could demand a meal from a senior’s home at any hour; a fighter pilot’s wife who saved her arguments for the weekend so her husband could fly without distraction; a 22-year-old MiG-21 pilot who didn’t know how to ride a scooter. “It was this very Indian world, a very grounded air force, rather than just the dashing fighter pilots that we see,” Parmar says. Srivastava initially wanted to make the story as a film; Parmar pushed for a series, despite neither of them having produced anything at that scale before. He turned Srivastava’s account into a 200-page pitch and sent it to Netflix India director of series Tanya Bami, expecting a pass. “To be very, very honest, I myself was very terrified when I saw these 200 pages,” Parmar says. Bami and the creative team came back with a greenlight in two weeks.
	

	To execute it, Parmar brought on producers from Matchbox Shots and requested a two- to three-week research recce to the real bases and the Kargil Valley before writing began, along with a crew chosen as much for its sensitivity to the human material as its ability to handle scale. That search led him to director  Sen, an advertising filmmaker who told Parmar he had never directed a car commercial because “it’s only machines,” and that what drew him to “Operation Safed Sagar” was its human core. The recce reshaped the writing, too: Parmar says it convinced him to break the sprawling material into modules, each functioning as something close to its own mini-series.

	Authenticity became the production’s organizing principle from there. “For us, authenticity was never optional. It was the foundation of this project,” Bami says. It’s the first Indian streaming production to film across active Indian Air Force bases, according to Netflix, shooting at Nal, Chandigarh, Madh Island in Mumbai and Gwalior, with access to operational MiG-21s and Mirage 2000 aircraft – likely the last unit to have filmed with the MiG-21s before their retirement. The team filmed at altitudes nearing 16,000 feet in Himachal Pradesh, at locations including the Shinku-La Pass, Jispa, Sissu and Rohtang, as well as the Drass Army base, to approximate conditions near the 18,000-foot heights where the war was fought.

	The series takes its title from the Air Force’s real operation name for the Kargil campaign; according to Parmar, fighter pilots looking down from those altitudes at the captured peaks described seeing an ocean of snow. Parmar says the production initially considered faking the conditions before abandoning the idea entirely. “We started doing deep research on where can the fake snow come from,” he says. “And one day, we were in a very deep discussion in our conference room saying which snow will give us the best texture. One person from the team said, ‘But what about the vapor that comes from it?'” That question, he says, spiraled into a recognition that nothing but the real altitude would capture how the actors would look and move, and the production ultimately shot at 13,000 to 16,000 feet with oxygen cylinders and ambulances on standby.

	Some 50 to 60 Indian Air Force and Golden Arrow Squadron veterans were consulted, including former Air Chief Marshal B.S. Dhanoa, and two former Air Force officers stayed on set throughout the shoot to oversee protocol, salutes and uniform detail, including tailoring that Netflix says was handled by Air Force tailors. “Even these small patches that you see on this uniform, they were actually built from actual Air Force vendors,” Parmar says. Group Captain Tarun Kumar Singha was involved from the earliest stages of story development, while Group Captain Alok Chaudhary coached the cast on cockpit body language and military bearing, uniform protocol and radio terminology. “Their excitement of having their first story being told at its authentic level is very high,” Bami says. “It’s been a deep, exciting collaboration.”
	

	Recreating the aerial combat required a comparable investment behind the camera. Netflix India director of production Ankit Gokani, who calls it the most ambitious show the platform has made in its 10 years in the country, says the series includes more than 50 minutes of flying sequences, developed first through more than a year of pre-visualization with over 10 vendors. 

	“The idea to do pre-visualization was really not to figure out just the tech part of it,” Gokani says. “The goal was, because a show like this is very technical to shoot, we didn’t want Abhijeet and Oni to be really figuring out how to get the technical stuff right on set, and instead concentrate on the actors because the heart of it is a human story, which we are looking to do.” 

	To get cockpit performances right, the production built a custom 2.7-tonne, six-degree-of-freedom motion base with MergeXR, shipped from Amsterdam, marking the first deployment of its kind in India. The rig was synced to an Unreal Engine pre-visualization pipeline, allowing actors to physically feel banks, dives and climbs that matched what would later appear on screen, with live compositing on set giving the director and cinematographer a real-time preview of the finished shot. “I still remember the first four days when the actors were just going through the simulations … the shock on their face because it felt very real for them,” Gokani says. The workflow cut cockpit filming from an estimated 30 days to 15. Gokani says visiting Air Force personnel mistook the constructed cockpit set for the real thing.



	

					“Operation Safed Sagar” Behind the Scenes
									Netflix
	



	The scale extended to the production’s footprint. Filming ran 115 days across 11 cities, including Patiala, Gwalior, Chandigarh and Bikaner, encompassing more than 100 locations, 190 speaking parts and temperatures ranging from minus 20 to over 40 degrees Celsius. “Getting people to feel the story and not get taken out of that experience was the toughest part for us,” Gokani says of the cockpit work in particular, adding that mounting a crew of more than 300 people safely at altitude “was a challenge on its own.” Netflix says the series engaged 850 local businesses, more than 200 cast and crew, and 4,000 daily hires, and worked with 12 to 15 Indian VFX studios, including yFX, Phantom FX, Atomic Arts, ZebuFX and NAC Studio, employing between 1,200 and 1,500 artists across Bangalore, Mumbai, Hyderabad and Chennai. Bami says the production deliberately kept the work in India rather than outsourcing it, building a first-of-its-kind VFX editor workshop, a custom color pipeline with local partners, and embedding an international VFX supervisor full time for more than two years to transfer expertise to Indian artists. She says the studio previewed a clip for Netflix leadership in Los Angeles earlier this year as an early test of how the material would land outside India.
	

	Netflix frames the series as a marker of its 10th year operating in India, tracing a line back to “Sacred Games,” the platform’s first Indian commissioned series, through titles including “Heeramandi,” “Delhi Crime,” “Kohrra,” “The Ba***ds of Bollywood” and “Taskaree.” “Every time we’ve really taken a bet on a distinct idea, on a new world, on a distinctive storytelling style, it’s something that the audiences have always been intrigued and curious about,” Bami says.



	

					“Operation Safed Sagar”
									Netflix
	



	“Dhurandhar” is the Aditya Dhar-directed Bollywood spy thriller starring Ranveer Singh as an undercover Indian agent infiltrating a criminal network in Karachi, a film largely set across the border in Pakistan. It became a worldwide box office hit before moving to Netflix, where it topped the platform’s chart in India and, notably, in Pakistan as well, holding the top spot there for weeks. That crossover came despite decades of tension between the two nuclear-armed neighbors, including three wars and a long-running dispute over Kashmir – the same fault line at the center of “Operation Safed Sagar.” 

	When asked how “Operation Safed Sagar” might land in Pakistan, Bami didn’t predict a specific reaction, pointing instead to the platform’s broader history of cross-border viewership. “As with all our stories, our focus is on telling compelling human stories through the lens of the people at the heart of them,” Bami says. “A lot of our titles are watched all over the world and they’ll hopefully resonate with this story, and they’ll engage with it. It’s a story of people, and it’s a story of the truth of those people. … Korean content is watched in India. Indian content is watched all over Asia and beyond. So I’m sure a story of this magnitude will be watched all over.”

	Parmar says he tried to stay faithful to the emotional throughline of the real Air Force officers and families he researched even where the show’s timeline required dramatic compression. “The focus in this story is the emotional growth of these characters that I’ve built,” he says. “But of course, some of the parts just didn’t fit into one timeline.”

	“Operation Safed Sagar” begins streaming globally on Netflix Aug. 7.

schema.headline: ‘Operation Safed Sagar’: Inside Netflix’s High-Altitude Bet on the Untold Story of the India-Pakistan Kargil War

title: Martin McDonagh to Be Honored at Zurich Film Festival as ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Receives Gala Premiere
description: The Zurich Film Festival will pay tribute to filmmaker Martin McDonagh as it gives a gala premiere to his latest film, “Wild Horse Nine,” starring J
body:
The Zurich Film Festival will pay tribute to filmmaker Martin McDonagh as it gives a gala premiere to his latest film, “Wild Horse Nine,” starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell.

	The London-based director will receive the festival’s prestigious A Tribute To … Award in recognition of his “outstanding contribution to cinema,” and will also take part in a masterclass in which he will offer “insights into his creative processes.”
	

	Christian Jungen, CEO of the festival, described McDonagh as “a master of dark comedy and character writing.”


	He added, “Through his personal signature style, he showcases a rare ability to captivate audiences through the interplay of meticulously crafted cinematography, atmospheric settings and clever storytelling, combined with an artistic intuition for striking the perfect balance between the absurd and the familiar. His wonderfully curious characters never fail to draw us in, and he has a remarkable gift for maneuvering them into absurd predicaments through screenplays of exceptional wit and precision.”

	“Wild Horse Nine,” which is set shortly before the 1973 Chilean coup, centers on CIA agents Chris (Malkovich) and Lee (Rockwell) as they set out to Easter Island from Santiago. There they are stationed alongside their boss and bureau chief, MJ (Steve Buscemi). Amongst the Island’s iconic statues, as the longtime partners wrestle with their dark pasts and present conspiracies, Chris’ newfound bond with a pair of rebellious students (Mariana di Girolamo and Ailín Salas) threatens to send everyone’s trip to this remote paradise sideways.
	

	Jungen commented, “McDonagh’s talent for eliciting complex and nuanced performances from his actors is a defining hallmark of his distinctive style. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ is no exception and, in our view, one of the standout films of the season.”

	McDonagh picked up Academy Award nominations for best picture with “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” and “The Banshees of Inisherin,” for best director with “The Banshees of Inisherin,” and for best original screenplay for “In Bruges,” “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” and “The Banshees of Inisherin.”

schema.headline: Martin McDonagh to Be Honored at Zurich Film Festival as ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Receives Gala Premiere

title: World Cup Boosts Fox Ad Sales in Q2, Profit Falls 3%
description:
Fox ad sales rose 78% (108% for the TV division) during from April-June due to the FIFA Men’s World Cup.

	Still, overall profit for the quarter dip
body:
Fox ad sales rose 78% (108% for the TV division) during from April-June due to the FIFA Men’s World Cup.

	Still, overall profit for the quarter dipped 3% year over year to $696 million. 

	Fox’s distribution revenue was up 7% to $2.03 billion from $1.94 billion year over year. Content and other revenues dropped more than 2% to $262 million from $269 million.


	Cable network programming revenue was up 9% to $1.67 billion. Ad sales for the division rose 22% to $83 million with the World Cup.
	

	Fox’s TV division saw overall revenue rise 45% to $2.5 billion. Ad sales were up 108% to $755 million due to the World Cup, digital sales at Tubi and higher political ad spending at Fox Television Stations.

	Corporate and “other” revenues came to $161 million compared to $63 million in the comparable 2025 quarter.

	Though the April-June period is traditionally the second quarter for companies, this marks the fourth quarter for Fox, which has a fiscal year that runs July 1-June 30.

	The company reported full-year revenue of $17.13 billion, up 5% from the prior. Year-long distribution sales were up 4%. Ad sales rose 7%, which Fox attributes to the World Cup and Tubi growth, which was offset by lower political advertising and comparison to the previous year’s results, which included Super Bowl LIX. Content and other revenue rose 4% on higher sports sublicensing revenue. 

	During a call with analysts Thursday, Murdoch said that Fox would not be making any changes to its current NFL deal until the pact expires after the 2029 season.

	Wall Street forecast earnings per share (EPS) of $1.34 on $3.6 billion in revenue, according to analyst consensus data provided by LSEG. Fox reported adjusted EPS of $1.79 on $4.2 billion in revenue. That revenue figure was up 28% from the prior year quarter.
	

	“Fiscal 2026 was an exceptional year for FOX, capped by our broadcast of a remarkable FIFA Men’s World Cup,” CEO Lachlan Murdoch said in a letter to shareholders. “We successfully launched our direct-to-consumer streaming service, FOX One, continued to keep America informed across a dynamic news cycle, enhanced Tubi’s position as a leading streaming service, and announced the acquisition of Roku which will transform the scope and growth profile of our company. Financially, these milestones were underpinned by the delivery of record top-line revenue which converted into record EBITDA. With strong momentum across our portfolio, we enter fiscal 2027 exceptionally well positioned to drive sustained growth and long-term shareholder value.”

schema.headline: World Cup Boosts Fox Ad Sales in Q2, Profit Falls 3%

title: ‘GTA 6’ to Debut ‘Extended Look’ on Netflix and YouTube on Aug. 27
description:
New footage of “Grand Theft Auto VI” will debut on Netflix and YouTube later this month.

	Per a press release from Rockstar Games issued Thursday,
body:
New footage of “Grand Theft Auto VI” will debut on Netflix and YouTube later this month.

	Per a press release from Rockstar Games issued Thursday, “Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look will premiere on Netflix Thursday, August 27 at 3 p.m. ET and will also launch on the official Rockstar Games YouTube channel and the Grand Theft Auto VI site at 9 p.m. ET on August 27.”

	In its own announcement, Netflix called the “GTA 6” collab “a first-of-its-kind partnership to premiere an extended look at the next evolution in the groundbreaking Grand Theft Auto series, Grand Theft Auto VI.” 
	

	The Rockstar Games-developed title has been in the making for 13 years. This “extended look” news comes after pre-orders opened for “GTA 6” in June with pricing set at $80 for the standard edition of the game.

	Per the synopsis for “GTA 6”: “Vice City, USA. Jason and Lucia have always known the deck is stacked against them. But when an easy score goes wrong, they find themselves on the darkest side of the sunniest place in America, in the middle of a conspiracy stretching across the state of Leonida — forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive.”

	On June 24, Take Two-Interactive-owned Rockstar Games revealed pricing for “GTA 6” would be $79.99 for the standard edition, which can be purchased as a digital or physical (which includes a code in a box rather than a disc) copy. The “ultimate” version will cost $99.99 and include “an exclusive collection of premium vehicles, weapons, apparel, and action threaded across all aspects” of the game.
	

	Rockstar has stated the launch version of the game consists of “a single-player experience set in the biggest, most immersive evolution of the series yet,” and has not mentioned a multiplayer or online component.

schema.headline: ‘GTA 6’ to Debut ‘Extended Look’ on Netflix and YouTube on Aug. 27

title: Versant Sees Q2 Profit Fall on Revenue Declines, Despite Ad-Sales Improvements
description: Versant Media said second-quarter net income fell by 30% as the new media company continued its efforts to add non-traditional assets to lend ballas
body:
Versant Media said second-quarter net income fell by 30% as the new media company continued its efforts to add non-traditional assets to lend ballast to its linear media operations.

	The owner of MS NOW, CNBC and USA said net income fell to $211 million from $302 million in the year-earlier quarter, a decline of $91 million. The company cited lower revenue, the costs of operating as a public company, interest expense following its separation from Comcast, and increased tax expense tied mostly to the divestiture of SportsEngine, an online sports management software company that was sold in May. 
	

	Versant said it was confident in its near-term future, raising revenue and cash-flow projections for the second half of the year


	Versant, spun off from Comcast earlier this year, is focused on generating new revenue from digital and direct to consumer operations. In recent weeks, it has expanded Fandango into a broader consumer entertainment platform, and made progress on new  subscription projects at both CNBC and MS NOW. “Together, we believe these initiatives build on the foundation of our portfolio, deepen consumer engagement, and position Versant for long-term growth,” said Mark Lazarus, the company’s CEO.

	Revenue in the second quarter fell 3.8% to $1.64 billion. Distribution fees fell 6.3% in the second quarter, largely due to subscriber declines. Ad revenue was off 0.6%, compared with a decline of 13% in the year-earlier quarter, reflecting improvements in ratings at some of its networks. Revenue from platforms, which include many of Versant’s direct to consumer businesses, rose 0.8%, due to higher revenue at Fandango and GolfNow.

schema.headline: Versant Sees Q2 Profit Fall on Revenue Declines, Despite Ad-Sales Improvements

title: James Gray Says AI Is ‘Worthless’ and Young People Won’t Stand for It: They ‘Have a Real Hunger for Interesting, Honest Stuff’
description:

body:
Over 30 years into his career, James Gray isn’t following any trends. And he’s not about to start now. 

	“This idea that we’re supposed to always try to be ‘new’… That doesn’t really mean anything. Many people say: ‘Oh, it’s important for a work to be fresh.’ The older I get, the more I realize that pursuit is a folly,” he tells Variety.

	“My tastes were formed in the late 1970s, and I was influenced by, inculcated by and taught by films from before that. It’s not a conscious effort to make a statement. It’s just an extension of who I am. I think it’s important that we embrace who we are, especially as we get older.”
	

	He adds: “If you look at Picasso, he stole from African art that’s thousand years old. Stanley Kubrick stole liberally from silent films, using ‘The Phantom Carriage’ for ‘The Shining’ and ‘Our Heavenly Bodies’ for ‘2001’. This idea that we have to create something ‘new’ is actually very much a business concept. It’s rooted in the idea of copyrights and capitalism, rather than reminding people of what is true: emotion, beauty and transcendence.” 


	“I like to say that what’s fresh in your refrigerator today is spoiled tomorrow.” 

	Since his feature debut “Little Odessa,” Gray has made, among others, “We Own the Night,” “Two Lovers,” sci-fi spectacle “Ad Astra” and “Paper Tiger.” In an industry caught between blockbusters and festival-only arthouse, his films sit in the middle. 

	“It’s true. It has caused me some agitation, but at the same time, it has been a superpower. This is not me saying that all art films are terrible, and I would love my films to make tons of money, but if that’s your only yardstick, then you want to eliminate risk – and risk is idiosyncrasy and subversion, and all the things that we treasure in movies.”
	

	“I’ve always thought it was beautiful to combine both. To have complex moral dilemmas for characters and situations within a narrative context. I don’t think I’d be getting my ‘old man prize’ if the films were either one or the other.”

	At Locarno, Gray will receive the Pardo alla Carriera lifetime achievement award.

	His approach has certainly tempted some of the world’s biggest stars, from frequent collaborator Joaquin Phoenix to Brad Pitt (“Ad Astra”) and, more recently, Adam Driver and Scarlett Johansson (“Paper Tiger”).

	“Directing actors is not about telling them how to say a line. It’s about giving them the space to be themselves, to be artists, to feel free in the moment, to listen, react and be in the scene. I do that for actors, and then the word gets out. I’m very fortunate that they all talk to each other,” he laughs. 

	“I didn’t know that Scarlett was, as she put it, a ‘rabid fan’ of my films. But I did know that she had checked up on me to find out what kind of director I am with actors. I guess the word is out that I leave them alone.” 

	Gray likes the idea of ensuring that his films are unmistakably his. 

	“It’s like with conductors such as Carlos Kleiber. Even with different orchestras, you can still tell it’s Kleiber. It has to do with the mood of the piece and the ability to express emotion in a certain register.”

	He adds: “Trust me – I don’t go on set and say: ‘I’m going to show the world that it’s me in this scene.’ That’s insane. But I think it’s good when I can see the director’s hand and when I recognize them just from a scene.” 

	“There are a lot of problems with auteur theory, but it’s great that you can identify a John Ford or Alfred Hitchcock movie simply from the placement of the camera and the pacing of the scene. That’s why AI is so worthless. It will never be able to do that.” 

	Even when working on a much bigger scale – he went to space in “Ad Astra” – Gray made sure his voice could still be heard. 

	“‘The Lost City of Z,’ which was insane, was a physical challenge. ‘Ad Astra’ had huge logistical challenges because you’re putting Brad Pitt on wires. But I never thought my own voice wouldn’t come through, because I wrote them. When you write your own movies, it’s very difficult not to have your own voice,” he states. 
	

	“There has been a bifurcation between the super arty and the super deluxe mainstream, and something in the middle is missing. If you look at Fellini and Kurosawa, that’s actually what they were doing.”

	“If you are in the middle, people accuse you of being middlebrow. It’s not the same thing! Expressing character dilemmas and complex ideas about morality, ethics and history within a narrative context is as subversive as it gets. If you are making something so arty and obtuse, or so commercial, what are you really subverting? ‘Vertigo’ was incredibly subversive. To me, that’s what lasts.” 

	Apparently, he’s not alone in thinking that. 

	“I may say something that will shock you. I have quite a bit of optimism, which I didn’t have even five years ago.”

	“This nightmarish side of AI has sharpened people’s idea of what it means to be authentic. Young people today have a real hunger for interesting, honest stuff that doesn’t feel jury-rigged to make a ton of money. I think that the reckoning is here,” he says. 

	“The studios are very confused. When they’re confused, and when you see a new generation coming in, sometimes it means weird stuff gets through the cracks. And that’s good.” 

	“I see my son going to revival houses to see ‘Il Sorpasso’ [1962 Italian comedy-drama] and it’s sold-out. That’s new. When I was a kid, revival houses were empty. It was just me and three homeless people sitting in the front row. There’s a cinephile culture that’s really exploding right now.”

	He’s not finished contributing to it, even despite that “old man’s award.”

	“That’s the thing: I’m not old. And I’m very gratified, but I feel like my best work is ahead of me. When he was my age, Hitchcock hadn’t yet made ‘Vertigo,’ ‘Psycho’ or ‘The Birds.’ My prime is right now.”

	He notes: “In total candor, I think it’s been very beneficial to me as a creative person not to have had instant, immediate, massive success. If I had, I’d probably be stuck in some rut. Instead, I’ve had a career that has hopefully steadily built in value.” 

	“I sit around and think about what’s important to express in a clear and unflinching way. I don’t think about how to match past successes. If you look at someone like Peter Bogdanovich, he made ‘The Last Picture Show,’ ‘What’s Up, Doc?’ and ‘Paper Moon,’ and then his work began to slip away. I’m only mentioning him because he said it himself. He said that success was harder to deal with than his failure.”
	

	Gray is very fond of “Paper Tiger,” however – an intense Cannes drama about two brothers caught up in a scheme that threatens their family. 

	“My son wanted to watch one of my films with me, and the prospect of doing that was so nauseating. Watching something you did 20 years ago is horrifying. But I very much like [‘Paper Tiger’]. I feel very close to it and I’m very proud of it, actually,” he admits. 

	“I do have many flaws, obviously. But not wanting to keep going is not one of them. I’m not done yet. Honestly, I feel like I owe the world one or two truly great movies. I don’t think I’ve gotten there yet.”

schema.headline: James Gray Says AI Is ‘Worthless’ and Young People Won’t Stand for It: They ‘Have a Real Hunger for Interesting, Honest Stuff’

title: Zaslav Admits Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Saga Has Been ‘Challenging’ for Employees but Claims Work Ethic Is ‘Inspiring’
description: What’s the mood among the Warner Bros. Discovery rank and file amid the pending Paramount takeover? Some WBD execs have privately expressed hope the
body:
What’s the mood among the Warner Bros. Discovery rank and file amid the pending Paramount takeover? Some WBD execs have privately expressed hope the antitrust case brought by 12 states, with a trial set to take place in March 2027, can slow down or stop the merger. Paramount and WBD had anticipated closing the deal by Q3 of this year.

	According to WBD chief executive David Zaslav, despite the uncertainty and delays with the merger, employees have displayed an “inspiring” work ethic to keep the business humming along.
	

	“The overall culture of this company and the work ethic of the company has been inspiring,” he said on the company’s Q2 earnings call. “It’s, you know, it has been challenging. … Our focus has been how do we drive a stronger company to meet our business plan and deliver a stronger and higher-growth company to PSKY and David, so that Paramount coming together with Warner Bros. is even stronger.”

	Zaslav said, “I thought it was going to be quite challenging, but you know when you look at the way this company is performing, and you look at the close to 40,000 people coming in every day — I went all across Europe in the last six weeks and … was in most of those countries meeting with people. They’re working extremely hard, and the focus has been that this is a great company, and that how do we take advantage of every day we’re here and try and focus on best performance possible.”

	He continued, “I’m quite inspired by the culture here and the drive to continue to put points on the board and take pride in the fact that that this is a great company and we want to deliver a great company. And I do think it’s unusual when you look at the overall performance of the company and how hard people are working, and so we’re lucky. I think that we have an unusual set of employees that really love these assets.”
	

	“And as long as we’re here, we’re going to be working hard every day to continue to honor Warner and HBO and Discovery and all the great assets on the DC side,” Zaslav said.

	Zaslav said DC Studios co-chairman and CEO James Gunn is focused on Superman movie “Man of Tomorrow,” set for July 9, 2027 release. Zaslav added, “I saw some pictures yesterday that looked amazing. Actually, yesterday was James’ birthday and he’s out working. He’s working 16, 18 hours a day. It looks fantastic. We’re super excited about it. Matt Reeves, I spoke to over the weekend, and he’s working very hard on Batman. And we have ‘Clayface’ coming up soon, which looks terrific. We got ‘Lanterns’ launching in the next few weeks on HBO, which which Casey [Bloys] and Sarah [Aubrey] are super excited about, and so DC feels very good, and we have a robust pipeline, and Peter [Safran] and James are hard at work.”

	Zaslav’s praise for the DC team comes after this summer’s “Supergirl” tanked at the box office, with the movie anticipated to lose $100 million. “Supergirl” ended its theatrical run with worldwide box office gross of $125.9 million (including $72 million domestically), the lowest haul for a DC movie in more than two decades.

	CFO Gunnar Wiedenfels told analysts that Warner Bros. is making 14 films this year, ramping that to 19 in 2027, and “we’re very confident that we’re going to be able to maintain that larger number. We have the unique benefit of a great creative team, great relationships in the talent communities, and an enormous amount of IP. So you know the way [studio heads] Mike [De Luca] and Pam [Abdy] and [DC Studios’] Peter and James are running this strategically is to find the right mix between, you know, original films, leveraging our IP to make, you know, the right number of tentpole IP-driven films.”

	Under the terms of the Paramount merger agreement, Warner Bros. Discovery can enter into bundling agreements and acquire content, and has the flexibility to negotiate extensions or renewals with existing partners (such as the NHL or MLB) as well as content-licensing sales as long as the deals don’t extend past December 2028. 

	On the call, Zaslav also reiterated his belief that Paramount will complete the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition in due course. If the Paramount Skydance-WBD merger closes, Zaslav is poised to walk away with a “golden parachute” payout of at least $550 million.
	

	“First and foremost, we’re confident this transaction will close, and we’ve been trying to drive the value of the company to deliver to PSKY and to David the best company possible,” he said. “The company is performing at a very high level, and we have every expectation that the transaction will close and that the company will be performing even better than the plan that we presented to PSKY when we did our deal.”

	In the second quarter of 2026, Warner Bros. Discovery total revenue fell 11% to $8.7 billion. Net income attributable to the company fell to $149 million from $1.58 billion, partially the result of $1.1 billion in “acquisition-related amortization of intangibles, content fair value step-up and restructuring expenses.”

schema.headline: Zaslav Admits Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Saga Has Been ‘Challenging’ for Employees but Claims Work Ethic Is ‘Inspiring’

title: ‘Primetime’ Trailer: Robert Pattinson Suits Up as ‘To Catch a Predator’ Host Chris Hansen in A24 Crime Thriller
description:
A24 has released the trailer for “Primetime,” giving a first look at Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen.

	The drama-thrill
body:
A24 has released the trailer for “Primetime,” giving a first look at Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen.

	The drama-thriller sees Pattinson step into Hansen’s shoes during a significant chapter in the history of the show, which followed Hansen and a camera crew as they executed sting operations designed to catch child predators. The official logline reads, “In 2006, ‘To Catch a Predator’ host Chris Hansen sets out to make television history.” 
	

	The cast also features Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo and Phoebe Bridgers.


	“To Catch a Predator” ran from 2004 to 2007 as a periodic special investigative report and primetime segment on Dateline NBC. The show followed undercover sting operations across the United States.

	In November 2006, Rockwall County assistant district attorney Bill Conradt killed himself as Texas police and the “To Catch a Predator” team entered his home with search and arrest warrants. Conradt had chatted with the show’s fake “child” actor, but did not travel to meet up. After the controversial incident, “To Catch a Predator” was canceled in 2008, following an investigation by ABC’s “20/20” and a lawsuit filed by Conradt’s sister. In its time on air, the show was massively popular, and the 2025 documentary “Predators” unpacked viewers’ fascination with the series and Conradt’s suicide.

	“Primetime” is scheduled for theatrical release on Sept. 25. The film is a Range Media, Icki Eneo Arlo and Square Peg production. Lance Oppenheim directed in his narrative feature film debut. Producers include Pattinson, Brian Kavanaugh-Jones, Fred Berger, Brighton McCloskey, Lars Knudsen and Tyler Campellone.
	

	Watch the full trailer below.

title: Fox Appears to Block NFL’s Effort to Re-Do Massive Rights Deal
description:
Did Lachlan Murdoch just tackle the NFL?

	The Fox CEO on Thursday surprised investors by announcing that Fox’s current deal with the National Footb
body:
Did Lachlan Murdoch just tackle the NFL?

	The Fox CEO on Thursday surprised investors by announcing that Fox’s current deal with the National Football League would remain as is through its end after the 2029 season, despite the league’s recent interest in using an “opt-out” clause baked into the 11-year pacts it struck with all of its media partners that would allow it to update terms to match market levels.


	“We don’t see any changes” to Fox’s current pact with the NFL until the 2030 season, Murdoch said during a call with investors. The company “will not be making any amendments” to the rights deal it has at present. Murdoch said the decision came after recent talks between Fox and the league, but declined to elaborate.
	

	The NFL has been in discussions with many of its rights partners, which also include Amazon, Disney, NBCUniversal and CBS, about updating its current contracts. The league has good reason to do so. It deliberately struck its most recent pacts with the opt-out clause, knowing full well that sports are one of the few things in the current media sector that continue to win the large, live audiences that advertisers and distributors crave. The value of sports deals continues to increase at an exponential rate — so much so that NBC is believed to be paying the NBA more for its current rights contract with that league than it is paying the NFL for “Sunday Night Football.”

	At the same time, the TV companies are no doubt loath to pay more money for their current NFL contracts, given the state of the industry. The rise of streaming has eroded the traditional TV business, with flows of revenue from advertising and distribution in general decline. Preserving a lower rights fee would serve the media companies well in the current moment.
	

	A spokesperson for the NFL could not be reached for immediate comment.

	The appeal of sports continues to play out in real time. Disney on Wednesday announced it had sold out all its commercial time tied to its 2027 broadcast of Super Bowl LXI — months ahead of the actual play date. TV networks with rights to the Big Game typically don’t unveil that status until the end of August or sometime in the fall.

	The NFL has also held what are believed to be serious discussions with Paramount Skydance about the status of its deal to show Sunday-afternoon NFL games. The change of control of the company, from the Redstone family to the Ellison family, gave the NFL the ability to open new discussions with CBS Sports.

	Spokespersons for CBS Sports, NBC Sports and Amazon’s Prime Video sports division could not be reached for immediate comment. The NFL cannot exercise an “opt-out” on Disney’s deal to show “Monday Night Football” on ESPN or ABC until after 2030. That pact has become more complex after a recent transaction that made the league a minority owner of ESPN in exchange for control of the NFL Network and other media assets controlled by the sports organization.

	Fox’s Murdoch said the company’s relationship with the NFL remained “incredibly positive,” and praised a recent transaction that gives Fox rights to show NFL games via its Mexican properties. Murdoch said Fox and the NFL will take up rights talks much closer to the of their current contract. If Murdoch is nervous about his ability to keep ties to the NFL despite what is likely to be a hefty cost increase, he wasn’t putting it on display. Fox, he said, sees “a clear path forward” after 2029.

schema.headline: Fox Appears to Block NFL’s Effort to Re-Do Massive Rights Deal

title: U.K. Approves Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger
description: The U.K. has cleared Paramount Skydance’s $111 ⁠billion acquisition of Warner Bros. on both competition and ⁠public interest grounds after Paramount
body:
The U.K. has cleared Paramount Skydance’s $111 ⁠billion acquisition of Warner Bros. on both competition and ⁠public interest grounds after Paramount beefed up promises ​about ​programming ⁠and news provision in the country.

	In a statement, the U.K.’s Department of Culture, Media and Sport said, “Today, the Competition and Markets Authority have announced their decision that there are no competition aspects of this proposed merger in the U.K. which necessitate their further intervention.”
	

	Among the areas that the CMA looked at were theatrical film distribution, linear children’s TV channels and the supply of subscription VOD services.


	The DCMS added that Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, had decided “not to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice on the basis that the assurances and further legally-binding commitments she has secured at this point from Paramount provide a set of protections that will help safeguard the continued availability of a diverse range of broadcasting and on-demand services in the U.K.; the continuation of their distinct editorial identities; and, the distinct editorial identities of key U.K. news programs.”

	The U.K. government received the following assurances from Paramount:


Media and streaming services: “Paramount set out clear intentions not to consolidate the Combined Group’s linear channels with its on-demand services in the U.K., and Paramount has made a commitment that they shall retain their distinct editorial identity.”




Children’s programming: “Paramount has promised that its children’s channels, including Nickelodeon and Cartoon Network, shall remain editorially distinct and continue to commission and acquire original U.K. children’s content.”




News plurality and editorial independence: “Paramount has promised to ensure that Channel 5 News maintains its editorial independence, that its editorial direction shall remain entirely separate from CBS News and CNN International, and that CNN International will continue to be available in the U.K. In addition, it has given assurances that the provider of Channel 5 News will continue to have editorial control and independence over news programming and that bona fide licensees will enjoy continued access to the CNN, CBS News and Channel 5 news archives on standard commercial terms.”




Channel 5 and U.K. investment: “Paramount has committed that Channel 5 will continue to operate as a Public Service Broadcaster fulfilling its PSB license obligations. Channel 5’s commissioning strategy will remain focused on the U.K., with Paramount committing more funding to support high-quality news, original children’s programming and drama.”



	Reacting to the U.K. decision, Paramount placed it in the context of its antitrust showdown in March 2027 against California attorney general Rob Bonta and his coalition of 11 other state AGs. “These conclusions further demonstrate the misguided and gerrymandered market definitions relied upon by the U.S. state AGs in their antitrust complaint in California,” a Paramount spokesperson said.

title: Arizona Man Catches Fire After Federal Officer Deploys Taser at Gas Pump
description:
Arizona Man
                          Tased by Officer at Gas Pump, Bursts Into Flames
body:
Arizona Man
                          Tased by Officer at Gas Pump, Bursts Into Flames
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 5, 2026
                            5:52 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 6, 2026
                                5:55 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Arizona man's fishing trip ended with him literally going up in flames ... after a federal wildlife officer deployed a Taser while he was standing beside a gas pump.
      
    
            Clarence "Chuck" Coyl captured the absolutely terrifying July 16 confrontation on video at a gas station on the Fort Mojave Indian Reservation ... with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service officer pointing a Taser at him and demanding his ID.
      
    
            Coyl asks, "What am I being arrested for?" ... and the officer tells him he's not cooperating after committing a crime.
      
    
            That's when Coyl fires back, "A misdemeanor? A misdemeanor?" and starts to say, "It's a ten-dollar--" ... before the unmistakable crackle of the Taser cuts him off.
      

            Seconds later, Coyl's phone falls, flames erupt, and he can be heard shouting in pain.
      
    
            Coyl says the wild encounter began earlier at Havasu National Wildlife Refuge, where he and a friend planned to fish. According to Coyl, an officer accused the pair of trespassing and told them to leave ... so they did.
      
    
            He then encountered the same officer again at the gas station.
      
    
            Civil rights attorney Ben Crump later posted another jaw-dropping angle of the confrontation ... showing the officer extend the Taser toward Coyl beside the pickup and fuel pump before flames suddenly burst beneath the truck.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Coyl says he plans to take legal action after he suffered first and second-degree burns and nerve damage to two fingers ... and local reports say he has not been charged in connection with the encounter.
      
    
            U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service confirmed its officer deployed the Taser ... adding it had no further comment on the matter.
      
    
            Coyl went out looking to catch fish ... and wound up catching fire instead.

title: Sydney Sweeney, Scooter Braun On the Ground Helping Washington Wildfire Victims
description:
Sydney Sweeney & Scooter Braun
                          Hometown Wildfire Relief
body:
Sydney Sweeney & Scooter Braun
                          Hometown Wildfire Relief
                          ... Lending a Helping Hand
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 5, 2026
                            6:51 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sydney Sweeney isn't just sending love to her wildfire-ravaged hometown from afar ... she's boots on the ground -- and Scooter Braun is right there with her.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... Sydney and her boyfriend are in Washington state amid the devasting Spokane area wildfires, with Sydney feeling compelled to head home and help any way she could.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Our sources tell us Sydney has been working nonstop since arriving ... bringing food to firefighters between shifts on the front lines and helping prepare and distribute meals to families affected by the fires.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            We're told they volunteered with Second Harvest Food Bank in Spokane and World Central Kitchen, personally handing out food and providing relief to people in need.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Our sources say Sydney has also been spotted around town buying groceries and working with local restaurants to secure food and shelter for displaced residents. We're told she has made major donations to multiple relief organizations as well.
      
    
            The trip hits especially close to home for Sydney. The "Euphoria" star grew up in Spokane and revealed this week the fires have affected members of her own family.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sydney posted an emotional message Tuesday saying Spokane has always been home to her ... adding it's where she grew up, where her family still lives and where many of the people and places that shaped her remain.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She said the fires have changed countless lives, including members of her own family, and urged her followers to donate as residents begin rebuilding.
      
    
            The fires around Spokane have scorched more than 10,000 acres, destroyed hundreds of structures and forced tens of thousands from their homes.
